passage:
Aadhya, you walk past that old stepwell every day and never look at it. Sit, and let your Amandeep Nanaji tell you its story.
Long ago, before my grandfather was born, there was a drought in our village near Patan. No rain for three years. The rich families had their own wells. The poor had nothing.
A widow called Roopba sold her gold bangles and hired diggers to make a well for everyone, with steps so even children could reach the water. People laughed at her. Then the water came, cold and deep, and nobody laughed again.
That is why, at every wedding in our village, the bride pours the first water from that stepwell. We remember that one person can care for everyone.

qa.q: What did Roopba sell to hire diggers?
qa.a: She sold her gold bangles.

qa.q: How did Roopba probably feel when people laughed at her?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt but determined, believing the well would help everyone.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Roopba's choice to spend her bangles on a well for everyone, because it saved the whole village in the drought.

qa.q: How might the poor families have felt when the water came?
qa.a: They would have felt deeply relieved and grateful, knowing someone had cared for them.

grounding: A grandfather tells his granddaughter a local history of the village stepwell and its moral of care.

passage:
The heritage walk through the old city of Hyderabad was supposed to take two hours. Then the rain came down hard, and the class had to squeeze under the arch of an old gate.
Noor, eleven, was annoyed. She'd wanted to see the palace.
Their guide, Madhuri, didn't waste the time. She pointed at the carvings above them. “This gate was built after a great flood. The people rebuilt their city together, rich and poor, carrying stones. Look, the carvings show their hands.”
Noor looked up. There were hands, dozens of them, carved in stone.
By the time the rain stopped, Noor had drawn every hand in her notebook.

qa.q: What did the carvings above the gate show?
qa.a: They showed the hands of the people who rebuilt the city.

qa.q: How did Noor feel about the heritage walk as the rain stopped it, and later?
qa.a: She felt annoyed at first, then curious and absorbed once she saw the carvings.

qa.q: What did Madhuri do that turned the rain into a good lesson?
qa.a: She used the time under the gate to tell its story and point out the carvings.

qa.q: How might the other students feel about the gate after the story?
qa.a: They may feel more connected to their city's history and see the gate differently.

grounding: Sheltering from rain, an eleven-year-old learns local history and its message of rebuilding together.

passage:
At bedtime in their Pune flat, Chandrika told Aadhya, nine, the story of the monkey and the crocodile. The crocodile's wife wanted the monkey's heart. The monkey was clever and said he'd left his heart in the tree, and escaped.
The next evening, Aadhya's little brother Neel was crying because a boy at the park had tricked him out of his ball.
Aadhya sat beside him. “Listen. Once there was a monkey…” She told the whole story, adding sound effects.
“So what does it mean?” Neel sniffed.
Aadhya thought. “Keep your head when someone tricks you. And don't trust everyone just because they're nice.”
Chandrika, listening at the door, smiled.

qa.q: Where did the monkey say he'd left his heart?
qa.a: He said he'd left his heart in the tree.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel listening at the door?
qa.a: She felt proud and happy, seeing Aadhya pass the story on.

qa.q: How did Aadhya use the folk tale to help Neel?
qa.a: She told the story and explained its lesson about keeping your head and being careful whom you trust.

qa.q: How might Neel feel after hearing the story?
qa.a: He probably feels comforted and a bit wiser about being tricked.

grounding: A nine-year-old retells a folk tale and its moral to comfort her little brother.

passage:
“Noor, can I really come to your Iftar?”
“Of course, Pallavi. Ammi said bring your appetite.”
“But you've been fasting all day. Aren't you starving?”
“A bit. But it's special. We fast in Ramzan to remember people who are hungry and to be close to God.”
“Do I have to do anything special?”
“Just wait till the call to prayer. Then we break the fast with dates.”
At Noor's house, Pallavi sat quietly as the family prayed. When the call came, Noor handed her a date. “Now.”
Pallavi ate it. “Thank you for letting me come.”
Noor grinned. “Next Diwali, I'm coming to yours for sweets.”

qa.q: What does Noor's family break the fast with?
qa.a: They break the fast with dates.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel about being invited to Iftar?
qa.a: She felt excited and curious, but a little unsure what to do.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do that showed respect?
qa.a: She asked what to do, sat quietly during prayer and thanked Noor's family.

qa.q: How might Noor feel when Pallavi joins her family's Iftar?
qa.a: She probably feels happy and proud to share her tradition with her friend.

grounding: A ten-year-old learns respectfully about her friend's Ramzan fast and Iftar.

passage:
Last year, I stayed over at my friend Irawati's house during Paryushan. I'm Swati. I didn't know much about it except that her family is Jain.
At dinner, they ate before sunset, and the food had no onion, garlic or root vegetables. I asked why, and Irawati's grandmother explained that they try not to harm even tiny living things during these days.
I felt a little embarrassed that I had brought potato chips as a gift. Irawati laughed and said we'd eat them another day.
That night, I watched her family sit quietly for their prayers. I didn't join in, but I didn't talk either. It felt peaceful.

qa.q: What did Irawati's family not eat during Paryushan?
qa.a: Onion, garlic or root vegetables.

qa.q: How did Swati feel about the gift of potato chips?
qa.a: Swati felt a little embarrassed, realising it didn't fit the family's practice.

qa.q: What did Swati do that showed respect?
qa.a: Swati asked politely, listened to the explanation and stayed quiet during the prayers.

qa.q: How did Irawati react to the chips?
qa.a: She laughed kindly and said they'd eat them another day.

grounding: A student learns about and respects a friend's Jain festival practices.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 6. Sunaina Das.
Before Gurpurab, Harpreet told the class about langar, the free kitchen at her gurdwara, where anyone can eat, sitting on the floor together.
Bhupen (eleven) asked many questions: “Can anyone come? Even if they're not Sikh? Why cover the head?” Harpreet answered each one.
On Sunday, Bhupen went with Harpreet's family to the gurdwara, covered his head with a scarf, and helped serve rotis. He told the class on Monday, “Everybody ate together. Nobody asked who I was.”
Next step: I'll invite families to share one festival each month.

qa.q: What did Bhupen help serve at the gurdwara?
qa.a: He helped serve rotis.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel about the langar after visiting?
qa.a: He felt moved and impressed that everyone ate together without being asked who they were.

qa.q: What did Bhupen do that showed respect for Harpreet's faith?
qa.a: He asked respectful questions, covered his head and helped serve.

qa.q: How might Harpreet feel when Bhupen comes to the gurdwara?
qa.a: She probably feels proud and happy that he wanted to learn about her faith.

grounding: A teacher notes an eleven-year-old learning about and respecting a classmate's Sikh practice.

passage:
Every evening at seven, Mohit's family in Nagpur lit a lamp and sat in silence for one minute, then each said one thing they were thankful for.
Tonight the power had gone, and a wedding band was blaring down the street. His friend Elizabeth was visiting.
“Can we skip it tonight?” Mohit's little brother asked.
Mohit, ten, shook his head. He lit the lamp with a matchstick. He closed his eyes. The trumpets were so loud he nearly laughed.
After the minute, he said, “I'm thankful for Elizabeth coming.”
Elizabeth hesitated, then folded her hands. “In my house we say grace. Can I say mine?”
Mohit's mother smiled. “Please.”

qa.q: What did Mohit's family do every evening at seven?
qa.a: They lit a lamp and sat in silence for one minute, then each said one thing they were thankful for.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel keeping the minute of silence during the noise?
qa.a: He felt calm but amused, nearly laughing at the loud trumpets.

qa.q: Why was it good for the family to keep the habit even on a noisy night?
qa.a: It showed the habit mattered, and made space for Elizabeth to share her own prayer.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel when invited to say her grace?
qa.a: She probably feels welcomed and respected for her own tradition.

grounding: A ten-year-old keeps his family's gratitude minute during a noisy power cut and welcomes a friend's prayer.

passage:
On the shelf in Pranav's bedroom in Bengaluru was a glass jar full of folded paper slips.
Every night, before sleep, his mother Madhuri sat on the edge of his bed. “Three things?”
Pranav, nine, thought. “Hot idli at breakfast. Kunal lent me his blue pencil. And the rain stopped before football.”
He wrote them on a slip and dropped it in the jar.
Some nights he couldn't think of anything and felt grumpy. Then Madhuri would say, “Just one small thing.” And he always found one.
On his birthday, they opened the jar and read the slips together. Pranav laughed at how many were about food.

qa.q: What did Pranav drop into the jar?
qa.a: He dropped a slip with three things he was thankful for.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel on nights when he couldn't think of anything?
qa.a: He felt grumpy until his mother suggested just one small thing.

qa.q: Why does the gratitude jar help Pranav?
qa.a: It helps him notice small good things each day and remember them later.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel reading the slips on his birthday?
qa.a: She probably feels touched and amused, seeing his happy memories.

grounding: A nine-year-old keeps a nightly gratitude habit with his mother.

passage:
“Payal, why are you sitting with your eyes closed? The bus comes in ten minutes.”
“Two minutes of quiet, Eshaan. Then I'll go.”
“Are you praying?”
“Sometimes. Sometimes I just breathe and think about the day.”
“Boring.”
“It's not. It helps me not be grumpy.”
Eshaan sat down next to her. “Show me.”
“Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly. Out. Think of one thing you're glad about.”
Eshaan was quiet. Then he said, “The bus is late. I'm glad.”
Payal laughed. “Close enough.”

qa.q: How long does Payal sit quietly?
qa.a: Two minutes.

qa.q: How does Payal feel about her morning quiet time?
qa.a: She feels calmer and less grumpy because of it.

qa.q: What makes Payal's quiet time an easy habit for Eshaan to try?
qa.a: It is short, simple and flexible, whether praying or just breathing and thinking.

qa.q: How does Eshaan's view of the habit change?
qa.a: He starts by calling it boring, then becomes curious and tries it.

grounding: An eleven-year-old keeps a short silence and gratitude habit and shares it with her brother.

passage:
First week of June: Suraj, ten, joined the colony cricket camp. He spent most of the time picking grass in the outfield. “Boring,” he told his aunt Rekha.
Late June: Rekha took him to a drawing class. He drew a cat, then a car. It was fine. He kept looking at the clock.
Mid-July: At a clay workshop in the community hall, Suraj made a small elephant. Then a bowl. Then a dragon with tiny scales. When Rekha came to fetch him, the hall was nearly empty and his hands were grey to the wrists.
“Already?” he asked. “Can I come again tomorrow?”

qa.q: What did Suraj make at the clay workshop?
qa.a: A small elephant, a bowl and a dragon with tiny scales.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel at the clay workshop?
qa.a: He felt so absorbed and happy that he lost track of time and wanted to come back.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that helped Suraj find his interest?
qa.a: She let him try different activities until he found one that absorbed him.

qa.q: How might Rekha feel seeing Suraj's grey hands?
qa.a: She probably feels pleased and amused that he has found something he loves.

grounding: Over several weeks a ten-year-old tries activities and notices what absorbs his attention.

passage:
Sarita, you want to know how I became an electrician? Let your Shalini Aaji tell you.
When I was eleven, in Nashik, my mother sent me to dance class. I tripped over my own feet. Then sewing. I pricked my fingers and cried.
But every evening my uncle, Dattu Kaka, sat on the verandah fixing radios. I would sit beside him, handing him screws. One day he let me hold the soldering iron. I didn't notice the sun go down. My mother had to call me three times for dinner.
People said girls don't fix radios. I didn't listen. Now look, forty years of wiring houses. Notice what makes you forget the time, Sarita.

qa.q: What was Dattu Kaka fixing on the verandah?
qa.a: He was fixing radios.

qa.q: How did young Shalini feel when fixing radios with her uncle?
qa.a: She felt so absorbed and happy that she didn't notice the sun go down.

qa.q: What choice in the story shaped Shalini's future?
qa.a: Choosing to follow her interest in fixing radios, even when people said girls don't do that.

qa.q: How might Dattu Kaka have felt about young Shalini's interest?
qa.a: He probably felt pleased and proud to share his skill with her.

grounding: A grandmother tells how she discovered her lifelong interest by noticing what absorbed her.

passage:
Nazia, eleven, stood outside the music room after school every Thursday, listening to the guitar class. Her family couldn't afford the fees this year.
One day, the teacher, Mr Tenzin, came out. “You're always here. Do you play?”
“No, sir. I just like listening.”
He looked at her for a moment. “There's an old guitar in the storeroom with only five strings. You can practise on it after class. Free.”
The next Thursday, Nazia sat in the corner with the old guitar, pressing strings until her fingertips hurt. When Mr Tenzin switched off the lights, she was still trying to play the first four notes of a song.

qa.q: How many strings did the old guitar have?
qa.a: It had only five strings.

qa.q: How did Nazia feel practising on the old guitar?
qa.a: She felt absorbed and determined, practising until her fingertips hurt.

qa.q: What did Mr Tenzin do that helped Nazia explore her interest?
qa.a: He noticed her listening and offered her the old guitar to practise for free.

qa.q: How might Mr Tenzin feel seeing Nazia still practising when he switches off the lights?
qa.a: He probably feels touched and hopeful about her dedication.

grounding: Despite little money, an eleven-year-old finds a way to follow the music that absorbs her.

passage:
In their Delhi flat, Tarun, ten, stuck two labels on two buckets under the sink: WET and DRY.
His sister Sarika laughed. “You think Mummy will use them?”
“She will if I help.”
Every evening after dinner, Tarun checked the buckets. Peels in wet, wrappers in dry. He took the wet one down to the colony's compost pit on Sundays.
He also started turning off the tap while brushing and switching off the fan when he left a room.
After a month, the family's dustbin bags went from two a day to one. Sarika started using the buckets too, without saying anything.

qa.q: What labels did Tarun stick on the buckets?
qa.a: WET and DRY.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel when Sarika laughed at his idea?
qa.a: He felt determined, sure it would work if he helped.

qa.q: Which of Tarun's habits reduced waste, and how?
qa.a: Sorting wet and dry waste and composting peels, which cut the dustbin bags from two a day to one.

qa.q: How does Sarika's attitude change?
qa.a: She starts out laughing but later quietly uses the buckets too.

grounding: A ten-year-old starts habits to reduce waste and save water and energy at home.

passage:
“Yash, you've left the fan on in your room again.”
“I'm coming back!”
“In an hour?” Hansa, eleven, switched it off. “Every day the lights are on in rooms nobody's in.”
“So? Papa pays the bill.”
“It's not just money. It uses power from coal. Our teacher showed us.”
Yash rolled his eyes. “Okay, Miss Environment.”
“Let's make a chart. Every room, every switch. Whoever leaves one on does the dishes.”
“Deal. But you'll lose first.”
By the weekend, Hansa had done the dishes once, and Yash three times. But the lights were off.

qa.q: What did Hansa suggest as a penalty?
qa.a: Whoever leaves a switch on does the dishes.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel about the lights left on?
qa.a: She felt annoyed and concerned about wasting power.

qa.q: Why was the chart a clever idea?
qa.a: It turned saving energy into a fun family game with a clear rule.

qa.q: How does Yash see Hansa's idea at first?
qa.a: He sees it as fussy, calling her Miss Environment, but agrees to play.

grounding: An eleven-year-old helps her family save energy with a fun switch-off chart.

passage:
I noticed it on Sports Day: a mountain of plastic water bottles in the bins behind the ground. Hundreds.
I'm Simran. I told my friend Hafsa, “We should do something.” She said, “What can two Class 6 kids do?”
We made a poster: BRING YOUR OWN BOTTLE. We asked the principal if the school could put a water filter near the ground. She agreed.
For the next Sports Day, everyone was asked to bring a steel bottle. Hafsa and I stood by the filter handing out stickers to anyone who did.
The bins were almost empty afterwards. Hafsa said, “Okay, two kids can do something.”

qa.q: What did the poster say?
qa.a: BRING YOUR OWN BOTTLE.

qa.q: How did Simran feel on seeing the mountain of plastic bottles?
qa.a: Simran felt upset and motivated to do something.

qa.q: What steps made the bottle drive work?
qa.a: A poster, asking the principal for a water filter, and handing out stickers to reward steel bottles.

qa.q: How does Hafsa's view change?
qa.a: Hafsa starts doubtful and ends convinced that two kids can make a difference.

grounding: A student starts a school drive to reduce plastic bottle waste.

passage:
The rain came down so hard that Joseph's parents called: the road was flooded, they'd be two hours late.
Joseph, eleven, was in charge of his cousin Santosh, six, who started crying as soon as the lights flickered.
“Stop crying,” Joseph snapped. “You always cry.” Santosh cried louder.
Joseph took a breath. He remembered how Ammachi calmed them when they were small. He lit a candle, sat next to Santosh, and started telling the story she used to tell about the fisherman and the golden fish.
Santosh stopped crying and leaned against him.
When the parents arrived, both boys were asleep on the sofa.

qa.q: How late did Joseph's parents say they'd be?
qa.a: Two hours late.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel when Santosh started crying?
qa.a: He felt irritated and stressed, snapping at him.

qa.q: What did Joseph do that calmed Santosh?
qa.a: He lit a candle, sat beside him and told Ammachi's story, as she used to.

qa.q: How might Santosh feel leaning against Joseph?
qa.a: He probably feels safe and comforted by his older cousin.

grounding: During a flood delay an eleven-year-old cares for a younger cousin using a grandmother's story.

passage:
Pranav and his sister Disha had fought over the window seat of the car all week, all the way to Nani's flat in Chennai.
That evening, Nani brought out a wooden board with fourteen pits and a bag of cowrie shells. “Pallanguzhi. I played it with my brother when I was your age.”
She taught them both. Pranav, ten, kept losing to Disha. He threw a shell.
Nani said quietly, “My brother used to throw shells too. Then he learned to count ahead.”
Pranav picked up the shell and watched Nani's hands. The next game, he won.
On the way home, he let Disha have the window seat.

qa.q: What did Nani bring out?
qa.a: A wooden board with fourteen pits and a bag of cowrie shells.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel when he kept losing to Disha?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and angry, throwing a shell.

qa.q: What did Nani do that helped Pranav?
qa.a: She calmly shared a story about her brother and taught him to count ahead.

qa.q: How might Disha feel when Pranav gives her the window seat?
qa.a: She probably feels surprised and happy, sensing the rivalry has eased.

grounding: A ten-year-old learns from his grandmother and eases his rivalry with his sister.

passage:
“Ammi, why does she get to sleep with you? I'm your son too.”
Sarika looked up from the baby. “Irfan, come here.”
Irfan, nine, came slowly and sat on the bed.
“When you were a baby, you slept with me too. Every night. You cried if I put you down.”
“Really?”
“Really. She's small now. She needs me close. You need me too, just differently.”
Irfan looked at his sister's tiny fist. “Can I hold her?”
Sarika showed him how to support her head. Irfan held her very still.
“She likes you,” Sarika whispered.
“She's squeezing my finger,” Irfan said, amazed.

qa.q: What did Sarika show Irfan how to do?
qa.a: She showed him how to support the baby's head.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel when he asked why the baby sleeps with Ammi?
qa.a: He felt jealous and left out.

qa.q: What did Sarika say that helped Irfan?
qa.a: She told him he had been cared for the same way and that he still needs her, just differently.

qa.q: How might the baby's arrival feel different for Irfan after holding her?
qa.a: He may feel more connected and protective, and less jealous.

grounding: A nine-year-old moves from jealousy of his baby sister to caring for her with his mother's help.

passage:
I thought I could study for the boards the way I did in Class 9: open the book, open my phone, and hope. I'm Anirban.
By January, I'd read the physics chapter four times and still couldn't solve the numericals. Kamal kept messaging memes every ten minutes, and I kept answering.
So I changed things. I made a timetable on the wall: two-hour blocks, with the hardest subject in the morning. My phone went into my father's drawer during each block. I told Kamal I'd reply at eight. He sent an angry face, then said, “Fair.”
I did past papers every Sunday, timed, like the real exam. My scores went up slowly.
On exam day, when the paper looked hard, I didn't panic. I'd seen hard papers before.

qa.q: Where did Anirban's phone go during each study block?
qa.a: Into the father's drawer.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel on exam day when the paper looked hard?
qa.a: Anirban felt calm and prepared rather than panicked, having seen hard papers before.

qa.q: Which change in Anirban's routine helped most, and why?
qa.a: Timed past papers every Sunday, because they built familiarity and calm for the real exam.

qa.q: How did Kamal react to Anirban's new rule about replying at eight?
qa.a: He sent an angry face at first, then accepted it as fair.

grounding: A teenager plans revision, blocks distraction and handles a high-stakes exam calmly.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 11. Vasudha Iyer.
In last week's mock exam, Karthik (sixteen) froze. He spent forty minutes on the first question, didn't finish, and left half the paper blank. He came to see me looking pale and said, “I know this stuff. I just panic.”
We worked out a plan together. First ten minutes: read the whole paper and mark easy, medium, hard. Start with the easy ones to build confidence. Set a rough time for each section. If stuck for more than a few minutes, move on and come back.
He practised it on two past papers. In today's second mock he finished with time to spare and scored much better.
Next step: follow-up before the board exams in March.

qa.q: How long did Karthik spend on the first question?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How was Karthik feeling when he came to see the counsellor?
qa.a: He was anxious and frustrated, pale and saying he panics.

qa.q: Why did the exam plan help Karthik?
qa.a: It gave him a clear order and time limits, so he didn't get stuck and could build confidence.

qa.q: How might Karthik's parents feel hearing about the second mock?
qa.a: They may feel relieved and proud that he has found a way to manage exams.

grounding: A counsellor helps a sixteen-year-old plan exam strategy to handle panic.

passage:
Wednesday night
Study group today at Karthik's. We tried something new. Thirty minutes of work, phones face down in a basket, then five minutes' break. Repeat.
First block: I kept glancing at the basket like it was calling me. By the third block I forgot it was there. We finished two whole chapters of chemistry.
Karthik made us each explain one reaction to the others, without notes. I got the second one wrong and felt stupid, but now I'll never forget it.
Exams in three weeks. I'm scared, obviously. But for the first time, I have a plan, not just a panic.
— Sabina

qa.q: Where did they put their phones?
qa.a: Face down in a basket.

qa.q: How does Sabina feel about the exams now?
qa.a: Sabina feels scared but more confident and hopeful, with a plan instead of panic.

qa.q: What study habits helped the group focus?
qa.a: Thirty-minute blocks with phones away, short breaks, and explaining topics to each other.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel about the study group's success?
qa.a: Karthik probably feels pleased and proud that the method helped everyone.

grounding: A teenager learns to resist distraction and plan revision in a study group.

passage:
I'm Farida, and I sit next to Chaitanya in Class 10. At the inter-school debate, I watched him in a way I never had before.
The motion was that homework should be banned. Chaitanya was against it. He didn't just shout his opinion. He gave three points, each with a fact: a survey from our own school, a quote from a teacher, and an example from his brother's school.
When the other side said homework causes stress, he nodded. “That's true for too much homework. So let's limit it, not ban it.”
The judges wrote a lot when he spoke. He came second. Afterwards, he said the other team's best point had made him change his closing line.
I don't know how he stayed so calm. I would have argued louder.

qa.q: What was the motion at the debate?
qa.a: That homework should be banned.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya seem to feel when the other side made its point?
qa.a: He seemed calm and open-minded, nodding and taking it seriously.

qa.q: What made Chaitanya's arguments strong?
qa.a: He gave evidence for each point and answered the other side fairly instead of dismissing them.

qa.q: How does Farida see Chaitanya's style of debating?
qa.a: Farida is impressed and a bit puzzled at how calm he stayed.

grounding: A classmate observes a teenager building arguments with evidence and answering counter-arguments fairly.

passage:
Before: In his first school debate in July, Naveen, fourteen, stood up and said uniforms were “stupid and useless,” then sat down. The other side said uniforms reduce show-off pressure. Naveen said, “No, they don't,” and nothing else. He lost badly.
During: Every Tuesday that month, Ms Neelam, the debate coach, made him practise one frame: claim, evidence, reason. “And then say what the other side will say, and answer it.” He hated it at first.
After: In the September final, Naveen argued for school gardens. He gave a survey, an example, and a reason. When the opponent said gardens waste time, he replied, “Some time, yes. But it teaches science and teamwork.” The audience clapped. His team won.

qa.q: What frame did Ms Neelam make Naveen practise?
qa.a: Claim, evidence, reason.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel about the practice frame at first?
qa.a: He felt annoyed and hated it at first.

qa.q: Why did Naveen do better in the September final?
qa.a: He used evidence and reasons and answered the opponent's point fairly, instead of just saying they were wrong.

qa.q: How might Ms Neelam feel watching the September final?
qa.a: She probably feels proud that her coaching helped Naveen improve.

grounding: Over three months a fourteen-year-old learns to build arguments with evidence and answer counter-arguments.

passage:
Aditi, you're preparing for the state debate? Come, let your Leela Nani tell you what I learned the hard way.
When I was seventeen, at a college debate in Mysore, my opponent was a quiet boy from a village school. He spoke slowly, with facts. I thought I could win by making the audience laugh at him. I mocked his accent.
The audience laughed. The judges didn't. I lost.
Afterwards the judge told me, “You didn't answer a single one of his points.”
The next year I faced him again. This time I listened, wrote down his points, and answered each one properly. I won by one mark. And he shook my hand and said, “That was fair.”

qa.q: Where was the college debate?
qa.a: In Mysore.

qa.q: How did young Leela feel after losing the first debate?
qa.a: She probably felt embarrassed and ashamed, realising mocking hadn't worked.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Leela win the next year?
qa.a: Listening to her opponent's points and answering each one properly instead of mocking.

qa.q: How might the village boy have felt when Leela mocked his accent?
qa.a: He probably felt hurt and humiliated, even though the judges saw it was unfair.

grounding: A grandmother tells how she learned to answer counter-arguments fairly instead of mocking.

passage:
In a pharmacy in Madrid, Rosa, fifteen, stopped at a poster for a face cream: 90% of users saw clearer skin!
Her friend Jin read the tiny print at the bottom. “Study of ten people. Over two weeks.”
“So nine out of ten people,” said Rosa. “That's… nine people.”
“And who chose the ten? The company.”
Rosa laughed. “And maybe their skin was getting better anyway.”
They looked at the price. Rosa put it back. “Ninety per cent sounds huge until you know it's nine.”
On the way out, Jin pointed at another sign: 50% OFF! “Off what?” he asked. “The price they made up?”

qa.q: How many people were in the study?
qa.a: Ten people.

qa.q: How did Rosa feel after reading the small print?
qa.a: She felt amused and more sceptical, laughing at how small the study was.

qa.q: What questions helped Rosa and Jin not be fooled by the number?
qa.a: How many people were tested, who chose them and whether the change would have happened anyway.

qa.q: How might the company that made the poster see shoppers like Rosa and Jin?
qa.a: The company may find them harder to persuade, since they check the small print.

grounding: Two fifteen-year-olds look past a percentage to question a small, biased sample.

passage:
In Class 11 maths, Ms Parul wrote on the board: Average marks in Section A: 72. Section B: 68.
“Which section did better?” she asked.
Most hands went up for A. Deepika, sixteen, hesitated. “Can we see the marks?”
Ms Parul smiled and wrote them out. In Section A, one student had scored 100. Most of the others were in the 60s. In Section B, most were close to 68.
“So one topper pulled up A's average,” said Deepika slowly. “Most students in B actually did about the same or better.”
Ms Parul nodded. “That's why we also look at the middle value, the median.”
Deepika wrote it in her notebook: Average can hide things.

qa.q: What was the average mark in Section A?
How did Deepika feel before asking to see the marks?
qa.a: She felt unsure and curious, hesitating before asking.

qa.q: What did Deepika's question reveal about averages?
qa.a: That one very high score can pull an average up and hide what most students got.

qa.q: How might students in Section B feel after the lesson?
qa.a: They may feel relieved and fairly judged, knowing most of them did about as well.

grounding: A sixteen-year-old learns how one high score can make an average misleading.

passage:
Hi Afreen,
You forwarded me that headline yesterday: TRAIN DELAYS DOUBLE THIS MONTH! and asked if we should stop taking the train to college.
I looked it up. Last month there were 2 delayed trains on our line out of about 600. This month, 4 out of about 600. So yes, it doubled. But it's still less than one in a hundred.
The headline wasn't lying. It just picked the scariest way to say it. “Doubled” sounds huge. “Went from 2 to 4” sounds normal.
So I'm still taking the 8:10. Save me a seat?
Darshan

qa.q: How many trains were delayed this month?
qa.a: 4 out of about 600.

qa.q: How did Afreen seem to feel about the headline?
qa.a: Afreen seemed worried, enough to ask whether to stop taking the train.

qa.q: What did Darshan do to judge the risk sensibly?
qa.a: Darshan looked up the real numbers and compared them with the total, not just the word “doubled.”

qa.q: What would change if the headline had said the delays went from 2 to 4?
qa.a: Readers like Afreen would probably not feel alarmed, because the small real numbers would be clear.

grounding: A teenager explains how a scary headline uses a percentage change that hides a small real risk.

passage:
Monday: A forwarded message in Vidya's class group said: Students who have a study lamp score 20% higher! Buy yours today! Vidya, fifteen, almost believed it. Her brother Siddharth said, “Maybe. But why?”
Wednesday: Vidya looked for the study. It was done by the lamp company. It found that students with lamps scored higher. But it didn't say whether those families also had quiet rooms, tuition, or more books.
Saturday: In class, she presented it. “The lamp might help a little. But the families who buy lamps may also have other things that help. That's correlation, not proof the lamp causes it.”
The teacher asked her to write it for the school magazine.

qa.q: Who did the study about study lamps?
qa.a: The lamp company.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel on Monday when she saw the message?
qa.a: She felt tempted to believe it, almost convinced.

qa.q: What questions helped Vidya judge the claim?
qa.a: Who did the study and whether other things, like quiet rooms or tuition, could explain the higher scores.

qa.q: How did Siddharth help Vidya think more carefully?
qa.a: He asked “why?” instead of simply accepting the claim.

grounding: Over a week a fifteen-year-old learns to separate correlation from causation in a sales claim.

passage:
Himani, you're laughing at your Dadu's lucky shirt? Let your Gurleen Bua tell you a story.
When I was sixteen, our village cricket team was sure that red socks made us win. My father wore red socks to every match. Everyone said, “See? We won again!”
I was curious. For a whole season, I kept a notebook: socks, weather, which bowler played, who won the toss. At the end, I counted.
With red socks: we won half the matches. Without: also half. But when our fast bowler Gurnam played, we won nearly every time.
I showed my father. He was quiet, then laughed. “So the socks don't bowl.” He still wore them, but we started paying Gurnam's bus fare.

qa.q: What did young Gurleen record in her notebook?
qa.a: Socks, weather, which bowler played and who won the toss.

qa.q: How did Gurleen's father feel when she showed him the results?
qa.a: He was quiet, perhaps surprised, then amused, laughing about the socks.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped the team, and why?
qa.a: Paying Gurnam's bus fare, because the evidence showed he, not the socks, was linked with winning.

qa.q: How might Gurnam have felt when the team started paying his bus fare?
qa.a: He probably felt valued and proud that his bowling was recognised.

grounding: An aunt tells how, as a teenager, she used evidence to test a lucky belief.

passage:
The science fair was the next morning, and at 9 p.m. Yusuf and Vikas, both sixteen, were finishing their poster: Plants grow taller with music!
Their data looked great. The three pots next to the speaker had grown taller than the three by the door.
Then Yusuf stopped. “Wait. The speaker was by the window.”
Vikas groaned. “So they got more sun too.”
“We can't say it's the music.”
They had no time to redo the experiment. Vikas wanted to leave the poster as it was.
Yusuf crossed out the title and wrote: Did music or sunlight help? We don't know yet. Underneath, he added: Next time: same light, only music different.
At the fair, the judge stopped at their table longest.

qa.q: Where was the speaker?
qa.a: By the window.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel when he realised the plants also got more sun?
qa.a: He felt worried and uneasy, but honest enough to change the claim.

qa.q: What was the right thing to do with the poster, and why?
qa.a: Change the title to say they didn't know yet, because sunlight could explain the result.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel about the change?
qa.a: He may feel frustrated at first, but relieved when the judge spends the longest at their table.

grounding: Under time pressure two sixteen-year-olds recognise a confounding factor and revise their claim honestly.
